# Appendix F: Comprehensive Index

*An alphabetical index of key concepts, organisms, researchers, and theoretical frameworks across all units. Each entry provides a concise definition and a pointer to the unit and chapter where the concept is primarily discussed.*

---

## A

**Action potential** — The electrical impulse generated by a neuron when its membrane potential exceeds threshold; propagates along the axon and triggers neurotransmitter release at synapses. *See: unit-08/chapter-25/neural-basics*

**Adaptive behaviour** — Behaviour that responds flexibly to environmental change in a way that increases the organism's probability of survival or reproduction; a key criterion in most functional definitions of cognition. *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.3*

**Allostasis** — Predictive regulation: the process by which an organism adjusts its physiology in anticipation of future demands, rather than merely reacting to current deviations. Distinguished from homeostasis by its forward-looking character. *See: unit-01/chapter-02/section-2.3*

**Altruistic punishment** — A behaviour in which individuals pay personal costs to punish defectors who violate cooperative norms, observed in social insects and possibly in slime molds. *See: unit-07/chapter-24/section-24.3*

**Amoeboid movement** — The form of locomotion used by amoebae and related protists, achieved by extending and retracting pseudopods in response to chemical gradients; a model system for studying directed movement without neurons. *See: unit-04/chapter-13/section-13.1*

**Anastomosis** — The fusion of two separate filaments or tubes into a common network; occurs in fungal hyphae and in *Physarum* networks, enabling resource sharing and network remodelling. *See: unit-06/chapter-21/section-21.2*

**Anticipation** — The property of adjusting behaviour prior to a predicted event, on the basis of prior experience with regular patterns. Demonstrated in *Physarum* (Saigusa et al., 2008) and in plants. *See: unit-04/chapter-12; unit-05/chapter-17*

**Associative learning** — The formation of a learned association between two stimuli (classical conditioning) or between a behaviour and its consequence (operant conditioning). Demonstrated in protists and plants under functional definition. *See: unit-04/chapter-14; unit-05/chapter-17*

**Attractor state** — In dynamical systems theory, a stable state toward which the system tends to evolve; used in gene regulatory networks and neural theories of memory to describe stable activity patterns. *See: unit-09/chapter-27/section-27.3*

**Autopoiesis** — The property of a system (such as a living cell) of producing and maintaining its own components and boundaries; proposed by Maturana and Varela as the defining property of living systems. *See: unit-09/chapter-27/section-27.1*

**Auxin** — A class of plant hormones (primarily indole-3-acetic acid) that regulate growth; directional gradients of auxin underlie phototropism, gravitropism, and root architecture. *See: unit-05/chapter-16/section-16.1*

---

## B

**Bacterial chemotaxis** — The directed movement of bacteria along chemical gradients via a biased random walk; achieved through the phosphorylation cascade of the chemotaxis two-component signalling system. *See: unit-03/chapter-08/section-8.1*

**Baluška, František** — Plant biologist and cognitive scientist; advocate for plant neurobiology; co-author with Michael Levin of "On Having No Head: Cognition throughout Biological Systems" (2016). *See: unit-05 introduction*

**Basal cognition** — The field studying cognitive-like capacities (sensing, learning, deciding, communicating) in organisms without nervous systems, and in non-neural components of organisms that do have them. *See: introduction; unit-01*

**Basin of attraction** — The set of initial states in a dynamical system from which trajectories converge to a given attractor; in gene networks, corresponds to the set of cellular states that develop into a particular cell type. *See: unit-09/chapter-27/section-27.3*

**Bayesian inference** — A probabilistic framework for updating beliefs in light of evidence; used in predictive processing accounts of perception and in models of bacterial chemotaxis as an approximation to optimal estimation. *See: unit-09/chapter-28*

**Bioelectric field** — The spatial pattern of electrical potential differences across cells and tissues, generated by ion channels and pumps; proposed by Michael Levin as an instructive signal for development and morphogenesis. *See: unit-02/chapter-05; unit-08/chapter-26*

**Biofilm** — A structured community of microorganisms (predominantly bacteria) enclosed in a self-produced extracellular matrix; exhibits division of labour, communication via quorum sensing, and collective decision-making. *See: unit-03/chapter-10*

**Biogenic approach** — Pamela Lyon's framework proposing that cognition is a fundamentally biological phenomenon, not an emergent property of brains; cognition is defined by the sensory-integrative-response triad present in all living cells. *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.4*

**Boolean network** — A discrete dynamical model of a gene regulatory network in which each node (gene) has a Boolean state (on/off) updated according to logical rules; used to identify attractor states corresponding to cell types. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Brownian motion** — Random thermal motion of particles; relevant to basal cognition because bacteria and unicellular organisms must navigate against or with Brownian noise; also a model for random search strategies. *See: unit-03/chapter-08/section-8.1*

---

## C

**Calvo, Paco (Francisco)** — Plant cognition researcher at the University of Murcia; co-editor of *The Oxford Handbook of Plant Neurobiology*; advocate for the hypothesis that plants engage in anticipatory, goal-directed behaviour. *See: unit-05 introduction*

**Calcium wave** — A propagating wave of increased intracellular calcium concentration; serves as a long-range signalling mechanism in plants (where it travels along phloem), in *Physarum*, and in many animal tissues. *See: unit-04/chapter-11; unit-05/chapter-16*

**Cellular automaton** — A discrete computational model in which cells on a grid update their states according to local rules; used to model slime mold dynamics and pattern formation in developmental biology. *See: unit-04/chapter-13*

**Chemoreceptor** — A receptor protein that binds a specific chemical ligand and transduces the binding event into an intracellular signal; the basis of bacterial chemotaxis (MCPs — methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins). *See: unit-03/chapter-08/section-8.1*

**Chemotaxis** — Movement directed by a chemical gradient; in bacteria, achieved by modulating tumbling frequency of the flagellar motor. Paradigm case of unicellular decision-making. *See: unit-03/chapter-08*

**Cognitive light cone** — Michael Levin's concept denoting the spatial and temporal extent over which an agent integrates information and makes decisions; varies enormously across biological systems. *See: unit-09/chapter-30*

**Collective intelligence** — The emergence of problem-solving capacity at the group level from the interactions of simpler individual agents; studied in ant colonies, bee swarms, and slime molds. *See: unit-07*

**Communication** — The transmission of information from one organism to another that alters the receiver's behaviour; distinguished from mere signal emission by its functional effect. *See: unit-07/chapter-23; unit-03/chapter-09*

**Competence** — In bacteria, the physiological state in which cells are able to take up exogenous DNA; regulated by quorum sensing in *Bacillus subtilis* and *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. *See: unit-03/chapter-09/section-9.3*

**Computational boundary** — The boundary within which information is integrated and processed by a system; Levin's concept, related to cognitive light cone. *See: unit-09/chapter-30*

**Connectome** — The complete wiring diagram of the neural connections in a nervous system; studied most completely in *C. elegans* (302 neurons). Provides context for understanding the transition to neural cognition. *See: unit-08/chapter-25*

**Consciousness** — Subjective experience; phenomenal states. Whether any non-neural organism has consciousness is a hard philosophical question that basal cognition research cannot resolve but must address. *See: unit-12/chapter-37*

**Cytoskeleton** — The internal scaffolding of a cell, composed of actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments; plays a role in cell movement, shape, and the transmission of mechanical signals. *See: unit-02/chapter-05*

---

## D

**Decision-making** — The process of selecting among alternative possible actions; in basal cognition, defined functionally as any process that produces a categorical outcome from a continuous input space. *See: unit-03/chapter-08; unit-01/chapter-01*

**Dennett, Daniel** — Philosopher of mind; author of *Consciousness Explained* (1991); his heterophenomenology and "intentional stance" provide a framework for attributing cognitive states to organisms without begging the question of phenomenology. *See: unit-12/chapter-37*

**Developmental plasticity** — The capacity of an organism to produce different phenotypes from the same genotype in response to different environmental conditions during development. *See: unit-05/chapter-17*

**Differentiation** — The process by which cells acquire specialised functions during development; involves changes in gene expression driven by transcription factor networks; connects to the attractor model of cell identity. *See: unit-02/chapter-06*

**Distributed cognition** — Cognition that is spread across multiple components (cells, organisms, artifacts) rather than localised in a central processor; relevant to ant colonies, biofilms, and plant root networks. *See: unit-07/chapter-23*

**Division of labour** — Specialisation of different agents within a collective to perform different tasks; observed in biofilms, ant colonies, and multicellular organisms. *See: unit-07/chapter-23; unit-03/chapter-10*

---

## E

**Efference copy** — An internal copy of a motor command sent to sensory systems to predict the sensory consequences of one's own actions; important in distinguishing self-generated from externally generated sensory events. *See: unit-09/chapter-28*

**Embodied cognition** — The view that cognition is not merely a matter of abstract computation in the brain but is shaped by the body's properties and its interaction with the environment. *See: unit-10*

**Emergent property** — A property of a system that is not present in any individual component but arises from the interactions among components; cognition in ant colonies and biofilms is often described as an emergent property. *See: unit-07/chapter-23*

**Enactivism** — A view of cognition, developed by Varela, Thompson, and Rosch, that cognition is enacted through the organism's active engagement with the environment; rejects the view that cognition is purely representational. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Epigenetics** — Changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in DNA sequence; includes DNA methylation and histone modification; potentially relevant to memory-like phenomena in plants. *See: unit-05/chapter-17/section-17.3*

**Ethylene** — A gaseous plant hormone involved in fruit ripening, senescence, and stress responses; its propagation through the air between plants can be considered a form of airborne chemical communication. *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

**Evolution of cognition** — The phylogenetic history of cognitive capacities; basal cognition research argues that sensing, learning, and communication are ancient capacities predating nervous systems. *See: unit-01/chapter-02*

---

## F

**Feedback loop** — A regulatory circuit in which the output of a process influences its own input; negative feedback stabilises (homeostasis); positive feedback amplifies (bistability). *See: unit-02/chapter-06; unit-09/chapter-27*

**Flagellar motor** — The rotary molecular machine driven by proton-motive force that propels bacterial flagella; direction of rotation (CW vs. CCW) determines running vs. tumbling behaviour. *See: unit-03/chapter-08*

**Foraging** — Searching for and acquiring food or resources; involves navigational strategies that in many organisms (ants, slime molds) can be described as optimal or near-optimal. *See: unit-04/chapter-12; unit-07/chapter-23*

**Free energy principle** — Karl Friston's unified theory of brain function proposing that all biological systems act to minimise their free energy (a proxy for surprise); extended to basal organisms as a framework for understanding goal-directed behaviour. *See: unit-09/chapter-28/section-28.4*

**Friston, Karl** — Neuroscientist at University College London; developer of the free energy principle and active inference framework; increasingly influential in basal cognition theory. *See: unit-09/chapter-28*

**Fungi** — Kingdom of heterotrophic eukaryotes including yeasts, moulds, and mushrooms; studied in basal cognition for their network problem-solving, chemotaxis, and communication via electrical signals. *See: unit-06*

---

## G

**Galvanism** — Historical term for electrical stimulation of biological tissue; modern descendants include the study of bioelectric fields and their role in regeneration and morphogenesis. *See: unit-02/chapter-05*

**Gap junction** — A protein channel (connexin or innexin) that directly connects the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing ions, small molecules, and electrical signals to pass between them; important in bioelectric signalling. *See: unit-02/chapter-05*

**Gene regulatory network (GRN)** — The network of interactions among transcription factors and their target genes that controls gene expression patterns; studied with Boolean and ODE models. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Goal-directedness** — The property of behaviour of being oriented toward a particular outcome; a central criterion in most definitions of cognition; can be described teleologically without implying conscious intention. *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.3*

**Gravitropism** — A plant's directed growth response to gravity; roots grow downward (positive gravitropism) and shoots grow upward (negative gravitropism). Involves redistribution of auxin. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

---

## H

**Habituation** — The simplest form of learning; a decrease in response to a repeated, inconsequential stimulus; demonstrated in *Mimosa pudica*, *Physarum*, and numerous unicellular organisms. *See: unit-05/chapter-17; unit-04/chapter-14*

**Hill coefficient** — A parameter measuring the cooperativity of ligand binding to a receptor; high Hill coefficients produce switch-like responses; important in gene regulation models. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Homeostasis** — The maintenance of a stable internal state in the face of external perturbations; achieved through negative feedback loops; proposed as a foundational form of proto-cognition. *See: unit-01/chapter-02*

**Hyphal network** — The filamentous network structure of fungi; can explore space efficiently, solve maze-like problems, and optimise connectivity in ways analogous to neural networks and human transport networks. *See: unit-06/chapter-21*

---

## I

**Information** — In Shannon's sense, the reduction of uncertainty; in biological sense, any signal that changes the state of a receiver in a functionally relevant way. *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.4*

**Information processing** — The transformation of input signals into output signals by a biological or computational system; a central concept in computational theories of mind and in basal cognition. *See: unit-01/chapter-01*

**Integrated information theory (IIT)** — Giulio Tononi's theory proposing that consciousness is identical to integrated information (Φ); potentially applicable to non-neural organisms with high Φ. *See: unit-09/chapter-29*

**Intentionality** — The property of mental states of being directed toward or about something; distinguishing intrinsic from derived intentionality is a central issue in attributing cognition to non-neural organisms. *See: unit-12/chapter-37*

**Ion channel** — A membrane protein that allows ions to flow across the cell membrane; the basis of electrical signalling in neurons and, more broadly, in bioelectric signalling in all cells. *See: unit-02/chapter-05*

---

## J

**Jasmonates** — Plant hormones derived from fatty acids; involved in defence responses to herbivory and wounding; can be transmitted through the air to alert neighbouring plants. *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

---

## K

**Kin recognition** — The ability to distinguish closely related from unrelated individuals; relevant to the evolution of cooperation; demonstrated in slime molds via the *csA* gene mediating selective cell adhesion. *See: unit-04/chapter-15*

**Kinesis** — Non-directed movement in response to a stimulus (intensity-dependent but not direction-dependent); contrasted with taxis. *See: unit-03/chapter-08*

---

## L

**Learning** — A change in behaviour or internal state that results from experience and persists beyond the duration of the experience; distinguished from adaptation and maturation. *See: unit-04/chapter-14; unit-05/chapter-17*

**Levin, Michael** — Developmental biologist at Tufts University; pioneering researcher in bioelectric signalling, morphogenesis, and cognitive light cones; co-PI of the Allen Discovery Center. *See: introduction; unit-02; unit-09/chapter-30*

**Lignin** — A complex polymer in plant cell walls that provides structural rigidity; relevant to basal cognition as a component of the physical infrastructure through which mechanical signals are transmitted. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

**Lyon, Pamela** — Philosopher and cognitive scientist; developer of the biogenic approach; author of "The Biogenic Approach to Cognition" (2006). *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.4*

---

## M

**Maladaptive behaviour** — Behaviour that is harmful to the organism's fitness in its current context; of interest in basal cognition because it constrains definitions of learning and decision-making. *See: unit-01/chapter-01*

**Mechanosensing** — The detection of mechanical stimuli (touch, pressure, fluid shear) by cells; mediated by mechanosensitive ion channels and integrins. *See: unit-02/chapter-05; unit-05/chapter-16*

**Memory** — The capacity to store and retrieve information from past experience in a way that alters future behaviour; in basal cognition, defined functionally without presupposing a substrate. *See: unit-04/chapter-14; unit-05/chapter-17*

**Metabolic memory** — A form of cellular memory based on the metabolic state of a cell (e.g., the activity level of enzymes or the concentrations of metabolites); proposed as a mechanism for learning in bacteria. *See: unit-03/chapter-08/section-8.4*

**Mimosa pudica** — The "sensitive plant"; a species of flowering plant whose leaves fold when touched; used as a model organism for studying habituation in plants. *See: unit-05/chapter-17*

**Minimal cognition** — The smallest set of capacities necessary for something to count as cognitive; defined by Pamela Lyon and others as: sensing, evaluating, responding. *See: unit-01/chapter-01/section-1.2*

**Modularity** — The organisation of a biological system into semi-independent modules that each perform specific functions; important for robustness and evolvability. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Morphogenesis** — The developmental process by which form is generated; controlled by bioelectric fields, chemical gradients, and mechanical forces; central to Levin's research on cognitive aspects of development. *See: unit-02/chapter-06*

**Motility** — The capacity of an organism to move under its own power; a prerequisite for most forms of behavioural response to the environment. *See: unit-03/chapter-08; unit-04/chapter-13*

**Mycelium** — The collective mass of hyphae forming a fungal network; can span large areas, solve transport optimisation problems, and exhibit coordinated responses. *See: unit-06/chapter-21*

---

## N

**Nakagaki, Toshiyuki** — Japanese biophysicist; lead author of the 2000 *Nature* paper demonstrating maze-solving by *Physarum polycephalum*; central figure in slime mold cognition research. *See: unit-04/chapter-12*

**Network motif** — A recurring pattern of connections in a biological network that performs a specific computational function; examples include feedforward loops, feedback loops, and coherent type 1 feedforward loops. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Neuroscience** — The scientific study of the nervous system; relevant to basal cognition as a source of concepts (learning, memory, decision-making) whose extension to non-neural systems is the subject of debate. *See: unit-08*

**Non-associative learning** — Learning that does not involve the pairing of stimuli; includes habituation and sensitisation. *See: unit-04/chapter-14; unit-05/chapter-17*

**Nucleus** — The membrane-bound organelle containing the genome in eukaryotic cells; its presence distinguishes eukaryotes from prokaryotes but is not the seat of cognition in any basal cognition account. *See: unit-02/chapter-04*

---

## O

**Open system** — A system that exchanges matter and energy with its environment; all living systems are open systems; their stability is maintained through continuous energy dissipation. *See: unit-01/chapter-02*

**Oscillation** — A periodic, repeating pattern of change; present in gene regulatory networks (e.g., the repressilator), in bioelectric fields, and in the rhythmic movements of plants. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Oxygen sensing** — The capacity to detect and respond to oxygen concentration gradients; relevant in anaerobic bacteria (which must avoid high oxygen) and in plant root navigation. *See: unit-03/chapter-08*

---

## P

**Perception** — The process of interpreting sensory information to build a model of the environment; in basal cognition, perception is re-conceptualised as sensory integration without presupposing representation. *See: unit-01/chapter-01*

**Phenotypic plasticity** — The ability of a single genotype to produce different phenotypes in response to different environmental conditions; a key adaptive strategy and a form of behavioural flexibility. *See: unit-05/chapter-17*

**Phloem** — The vascular tissue in plants that transports photosynthetic products (sucrose) and signalling molecules (including RNA and calcium waves) from leaves to roots and growing regions. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

**Phototropism** — Directed growth toward (or away from) a light source; mediated by auxin redistribution in response to blue light detected by phototropin receptors. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

**Physarum polycephalum** — A plasmodial slime mold (myxomycete); the central model organism for basal cognition research; demonstrated to solve mazes, optimise networks, and habituate to stimuli. *See: unit-04/chapter-12*

**Plasmid** — A small circular DNA molecule in bacteria that can be transmitted horizontally; relevant to quorum sensing research because many QS genes are plasmid-encoded. *See: unit-03/chapter-09*

**Protist** — A diverse group of eukaryotic microorganisms that are not animals, plants, or fungi; includes amoebae, ciliates, and flagellates; central study organisms in basal cognition. *See: unit-04*

**Pseudopod** — A temporary extension of the cell membrane used for movement and food capture in amoebae; their directed extension toward food sources is a paradigm of chemotaxis without neurons. *See: unit-04/chapter-13*

---

## Q

**Quorum sensing** — The process by which bacteria detect their population density through the accumulation of signalling molecules (autoinducers) and coordinate gene expression once a threshold is reached. *See: unit-03/chapter-09*

---

## R

**Reactive oxygen species (ROS)** — Chemically reactive molecules containing oxygen (e.g., superoxide, hydrogen peroxide); produced during stress responses in plants and bacteria; serve as long-range signals. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

**Receptive field** — In sensory neuroscience, the region of the environment to which a neuron responds; by extension, the domain of stimuli to which a cell or organism responds; applied to plant and fungal sensory systems. *See: unit-08/chapter-25*

**Regeneration** — The regrowth of lost or damaged tissue; relevant to basal cognition through Levin's work on bioelectric control of regeneration in planarians and other organisms. *See: unit-02/chapter-06*

**Repressilator** — A synthetic gene circuit constructed by Elowitz and Leibler (2000) consisting of three mutually repressing genes that produce oscillatory gene expression; a landmark in synthetic biology. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Robustness** — The ability of a system to maintain its function in the face of perturbations (noise, mutations, environmental changes); a key design principle in biological regulatory networks. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

---

## S

**Salicylic acid** — A plant hormone involved in systemic acquired resistance; when one part of a plant is infected, salicylic acid signals spread to other parts, priming defences against further attack. *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

**Sensitisation** — An increase in response to a stimulus following prior exposure to a noxious stimulus; the opposite of habituation; a form of non-associative learning. *See: unit-04/chapter-14*

**Signal transduction** — The process by which a cell converts an extracellular signal (ligand binding, mechanical force) into an intracellular response; the molecular basis of all cellular sensing. *See: unit-02/chapter-05*

**Slime mold** — Common name for several unrelated groups of amoeboid eukaryotes; includes cellular slime molds (*Dictyostelium discoideum*) and plasmodial slime molds (*Physarum polycephalum*). *See: unit-04*

**Soma** — The cell body of a neuron, containing the nucleus; by extension, sometimes used to refer to the main body of an organism as opposed to its projections. *See: unit-08/chapter-25*

**Sporulation** — The formation of spores, highly resistant dormant structures, as a survival strategy under adverse conditions; the decision to sporulate in *Bacillus subtilis* involves quorum sensing and complex regulatory networks. *See: unit-03/chapter-10*

**Stochastic** — Involving randomness; stochastic gene expression (random fluctuations in gene product numbers) is a source of phenotypic variability and is relevant to decision-making in bacteria. *See: unit-03/chapter-08; unit-09/chapter-27*

**Stigmergy** — A mechanism of indirect coordination in which the actions of one agent modify the environment in a way that guides the actions of subsequent agents; the basis of many collective intelligence phenomena (ant pheromone trails, slime mold network formation). *See: unit-07/chapter-23*

**Symbiosis** — A long-term, close interaction between two organisms of different species; includes mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism; the mycorrhizal network is a paradigm case relevant to basal cognition. *See: unit-06/chapter-22*

**Systemic acquired resistance (SAR)** — A plant immunity response triggered by local infection that results in broad, long-lasting resistance throughout the plant. *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

---

## T

**Taxis** — Directed movement toward or away from a stimulus; examples include chemotaxis, phototaxis, gravitaxis. The direction of movement depends on the direction of the gradient. *See: unit-03/chapter-08*

**Threshold** — In signalling, the minimum stimulus intensity required to trigger a response; thresholds create switch-like behaviour and are important in quorum sensing and action potential generation. *See: unit-03/chapter-09; unit-08/chapter-25*

**Tononi, Giulio** — Neuroscientist and consciousness researcher; developer of integrated information theory (IIT). *See: unit-09/chapter-29*

**Transcription factor** — A protein that binds DNA and regulates the expression of downstream genes; the primary effector of gene regulatory networks. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Tropism** — A directed growth response of a plant to an environmental stimulus; includes phototropism, gravitropism, thigmotropism (touch), and hydrotropism (water). *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

**Turing, Alan** — Mathematician and computer scientist; his reaction-diffusion model of morphogenesis (1952) is a foundational contribution to mathematical biology and to the study of self-organisation in biological systems. *See: unit-02/chapter-06*

**Two-component signalling** — A widespread signal transduction mechanism in bacteria consisting of a sensor histidine kinase and a response regulator; the molecular basis of bacterial chemotaxis. *See: unit-03/chapter-08/section-8.1*

---

## U

**Umwelt** — Jakob von Uexküll's concept of the subjective, species-specific sensory world of an organism; each organism has access to only those aspects of the environment that are relevant to its sensory and motor capacities. *See: unit-01/chapter-02; unit-12/chapter-36*

---

## V

**Varela, Francisco** — Chilean biologist and philosopher; co-developer of autopoiesis theory and enactivism; major influence on theories of basal cognition. *See: unit-09/chapter-27*

**Vesicle** — A small membrane-bound compartment within a cell; secretory vesicles carry neurotransmitters and signalling molecules to the cell surface for release. *See: unit-02/chapter-04*

**Volatile organic compound (VOC)** — A carbon-containing compound that evaporates at room temperature; used by plants for airborne communication (including the "crying out" of wounded plants). *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

---

## W

**Wood wide web** — The colloquial term for the mycorrhizal fungal network connecting the roots of multiple trees and plants in a forest, enabling transfer of carbon, water, and signalling molecules. *See: unit-06/chapter-22*

**Wound signalling** — The propagation of signals from wounded plant tissue to distal parts of the plant, triggering defensive responses; mediated by jasmonates, electrical signals, and calcium waves. *See: unit-05/chapter-19*

---

## X

**Xenobiology** — The study of biological systems based on alternative chemistries or substrates; relevant to basal cognition as a framework for asking whether cognition is substrate-independent. *See: unit-13/chapter-40*

---

## Y

**Xylem** — The vascular tissue in plants that transports water and dissolved minerals from roots to shoots; also transmits electrical and hydraulic signals over long distances. *See: unit-05/chapter-16*

---

## Z

**Zooplankton** — Microscopic animals drifting in aquatic environments; many exhibit sophisticated chemotaxis and predator-avoidance behaviours without complex nervous systems. *See: unit-04/chapter-13*

---

*This index covers the principal concepts of all thirteen units. For exhaustive chapter-level citations, consult the individual unit READMEs and chapter files.*
